description: Evidence packs in the shapes a deployment hands them over in, the keys a reader designates beside each one, and the verdict the shipped pack reader owes: whole documents accepted with the run and the window reported apart, the per-item provenance values their material states reduced to the pack's own, the references a pack signs for each held slot its sealed receipts name, an honest pack whose stamps run against its links reported and not refused, and one refusal for every fault the format names.

layout.writer: signPack in @ashaveri/receipt, which every honest seal here went through, and encodePackManifest, encodePackProtectedHeader, packSigStructure and sealPack, which assembled the rows that writer refuses to sign
layout.reader: verifyPack in @ashaveri/receipt, which is the verdict column, and decodePack, which is the structural column and needs no key
layout.headerCloses: the protected header carries exactly the three labels above and no fourth, because its bytes are hashed into the signature; every map inside the payload closes the same way
layout.sigStructure: RFC 9052 section 4.4: the array ["Signature1", the protected bstr as written, the external AAD, the payload bstr], canonically encoded. The external AAD is empty for this container and nothing inside the envelope carries which one was used.
layout.recordDigest: sha256 over 0x00 || prev || iat as eight big-endian bytes || the byte length of id as two big-endian bytes || id || receipt bytes. Every integer in that input is unsigned and big-endian, which is the framing section 5.2 publishes and the images in chain-v1.json show.
layout.chainRule: the walk starts at the item whose prev is the signed anchor, recomputes each record digest from the bytes the item carries, and ends at the signed head; every item of the array has to be reached, which is the second half of the rule and the only one with eyes for a receipt parked beside a run it is not part of
layout.spanRule: the span is half-open, from included and to excluded, and both bounds bind every item. at is never before to, and duty.rev is never after at
layout.dutyRule: held is at least the age of the oldest receipt in this pack, measured at at. A held short of required is nothing of that kind: the document is whole and the reader states no verdict on the duty, because met is absent from the format on purpose
layout.orderingRule: the links fix the order of the run and an item iat is the stamp that record was chained under, and the two are free to disagree because the store chains under whatever stamp it was handed. A reader reports a disagreement on the result and never refuses it: the lawful output of a deployment that corrected its clock is a pack with the finding beside a clean walk
layout.provenanceRule: the three values are live, captured and fixture, written in the format's strength order, and a pack's own prov is the weakest of its items' values: a value that is not the reduction, in either direction, is refused under PACK_BAD_MANIFEST, so a pack cannot be assembled to claim live while carrying one fixture. Live software never becomes hardware evidence, because a run of live items reduces to live and never to captured, and a captured original can retain valid hardware evidence, because a captured item beside live ones keeps the captured value rather than being washed down to live. The field is separate from execution assurance, from the custody references and from the duty: what a receipt's meas and att claim, what an anchor names and what period the window answers under are three other questions, and since no reader recomputes where material came from, the field is one statement a reader checks against the items and never a verdict about their bytes
layout.custodyRule: custody holds one reference per named held slot of a sealed receipt, and a reference states where it was read from, what was asked, what the answer said it was, when its last byte landed and what that source declares about itself, the digest of the body, the digest of the header that arrived beside it, which arm weighed them and the window the document signed for itself. attached holds the material itself, whole, where a deployment attaches it: the bytes, their digest, and a header beside them exactly when the digest of that header is stated. The reader recomputes each digest instead of trusting the statement beside it, refuses a list of references past the 2 slots every sealed receipt can name, an attached object past the 65535 bytes the format already states for a run of bytes, an attachment past that same count of slots, an instant that is no whole number of Unix seconds inside the band the receipt format draws, and the pair of lists and the slots failing to speak of the same material: no entry answering for a slot no sealed receipt states, no held slot no reference answers for, no digest attached at two positions, no object the body digest of no reference names, and no header carried beside a reference that states none. A slot that states an absence names no digest and owes no reference and no bytes, so a pack referring to nothing and attaching nothing for a run of absences is whole. Each refusal names the position it found
layout.encodings: documents and byte strings unpadded base64url, digests, kids, predecessors and signatures lowercase hex, instants unix seconds
layout.verdictMeaning: `verdict` is what verifyPack answers under the designation the row states: `verify-ok`, or the code it throws. `structural` is what decodePack answers for the same bytes with no key, so a row that is `verify-ok` there and a refusal in `verdict` is refusing about a key or a signature and not about a manifest that contradicts itself. `walk` is the order the links reached and `ordering` the steps where the stamps disagree; both are published on every accepted row.
layout.readFields: `read.pinned` is the one key the caller holds, which designates the envelope and every receipt inside it. `read.retained` is the set a resolver answers from, one key per kid, which is how a span crossing a rotation is read. A row with neither is the call that designated nothing and is refused before a byte is read.
layout.framingRule: records frames the run of `well-formed-three-items` and attachedRecords frames the run of `held-slots-referred-to-by-name`, and those are the two runs this suite publishes a framing for: the canonical run, whose every slot of every sealed receipt states an absence, and the run whose every held slot is answered by a reference the pack signs. A row beside them is read the same way and framed by the same rule, so what the two tables give a port is two published answers to recompute against rather than one. Each row of a table is derived from the sealed bytes of the document it sits beside rather than from the manifest its writer was handed, so a table cannot describe a run the published document does not hold
layout.assembled: every honest pack is `signPack` and no hand-built bytes. Where a row needs something that writer refuses to sign, the manifest is encoded, one position of its map is changed, and the result is signed over the published `Sig_structure` and sealed by `sealPack` under the key its header names; the generator stops unless that path reproduces `signPack` byte for byte on the canonical header, so each fault below is the one position its `edited` field names and nothing else. The writer is also asked to sign a manifest that contradicts its own span, a pack under a key whose kid is not sha256 of its public half, a pack whose own provenance is not the weakest of its items, and each position the reference list and the byte arm can disagree with the slots their sealed receipts name, and refuses all of them with the code the row publishes, which is why this suite carries no row that a deployment could have produced by accident. The generator also walks every combination of three items' provenance values through the reduction, seals the pack the same builder computes, and asks the reader for the same three values back; and one accepted row does attach material: `custody-served-weighed` hands over a served body and the issuer-chain header that arrived beside it, both made here by the fixture vendor this repository generates, because a reference resolving to nothing is a claim no port can be weighed against. The generator decodes every accepted document, resolves each object of its arm by the digest recomputed from the bytes beside it, and stops unless a reference of that same pack names that digest and states the same digest for any header attached with it; an object no reference names appears only in a row the reader refuses.

keyMaterial.seed: sha256 of 'ashaveri-fixtures/receipt-key/v1', the committed fixture receipt key
keyMaterial.role: seals the honest packs and signs the receipts inside them
the epoch superseded inside a span, whose receipts the pack still carries
another deployment's key, for the pack sealed under a key its caller does not designate and the signature not made by the key its header names

layout.keyNote: test-only, published so a port can produce these signatures itself rather than only checking them, and protecting nothing. The honest packs here are sealed by the same key the committed receipt fixtures are issued under, which is the key a deployment names in its manifest and the one a reader of a pack is handed for the receipts inside it.

vectors.name: well-formed-three-items
vectors.note: Three receipts chained from an anchor of thirty-two zero bytes to a head inside the signature, sealed by the key that signed every receipt in the container, and read by a caller that pinned that key. This is the state a handover arrives in and everything a reader is entitled to say about it: the run the links fix, and the window the manifest states, as two separate findings.

vectors.name: array-order-bears-nothing
vectors.note: The same pack with its items handed over in the reverse of the order the chain puts them. The walk starts at the item naming the anchor and follows the links, so the run it reports is the run it would have reported, which is the rule that keeps a retirement or a compaction from having to rewrite an array.

vectors.name: retired-prefix-behind-a-seam
vectors.note: A run that began after a retirement, chained from the seam the trim record carried rather than from zero bytes. The anchor arrives as the same member either way and a reader does not have to know which happened to start walking.

vectors.name: single-item-pack
vectors.note: One receipt, which is a whole walk rather than a degenerate one: the item whose `prev` is the anchor is first and the item whose own digest is the head is last, and here they are the same item. The format refuses a pack with no items at all, because a walk over nothing closes vacuously and would read as evidence.

vectors.name: span-crossing-a-key-rotation
vectors.note: The receipts of the epoch a deployment retired inside the window, beside those of the key that replaced it, sealed by the current one. A caller that hands the reader the keys it retained reads the whole run; each item verifies under the key its own header names, and the envelope under the one that signed it.

vectors.name: rotation-read-with-one-pinned-key
vectors.note: Those same bytes read by a caller that retained only the current epoch. The envelope verifies and the first item does not, and the refusal names the item and the answer its own receipt gave, because the pack is not the thing at fault: the caller is holding too few keys.

vectors.name: rotation-read-without-the-retired-epoch
vectors.note: The same span and a resolver that answers for the current kid only. This is the one inner refusal the reader does not keep as a receipt's answer: nothing about the pack contradicts itself, and the action is to go and retain the key the deployment's manifest names rather than to refuse these bytes.

vectors.name: held-slots-referred-to-by-name
vectors.note: Three receipts whose anchors name material, and the pack that answers each held slot with a reference and attaches nothing. The `col` digest all three records name is three references rather than one, because a reference answers for the slot it names and not for the digest it shares, and each states the declaration it read, the request as asked, the instant the last byte landed, the body digest its slot digests and the digest of the header that arrived beside it where the weighing read one. A reader holding this pack learns what was seen, by which arm, and when, and reaches no endpoint to learn it. The pack states no verdict about those bytes and hands on none of them.

vectors.name: one-observation-answers-both-held-slots
vectors.note: One sealed receipt whose `col` and `val` slots digest the same body, because the document this appraisal took in as its collateral states the window its validity half names, and the pack that answers the pair with two references. Their stated body digests are equal and their keys are not, which is what it means for a reference to answer a slot rather than the material a slot digests: the list is read one held slot at a time, and two slots of one record are two positions in it even where one reading produced both. The pack attaches nothing beside them.

vectors.name: custody-served-weighed
vectors.note: The run whose `col` slot all three records name is a served answer, and this pack attaches it: the body as the origin sent it, a wrapper holding the document member and a hex signature member, beside the issuer-chain header that arrived with it, plus the two embedded readings the `val` slots name and no header for. Six references answer six held slots, three of them stating the same body digest and the same digest of the header that arrived beside it, and the arm holds that object once. The reader recomputes every digest in the container, so this row is the answer for the case every port is meant to reach: a reference resolving to material the reader can weigh, at the instant the naming record was chained at, with no endpoint consulted. Both halves of the pair were made by this repository's own fixture vendor, so a reader may pin its root and read a window and a status out of them; the pack itself states no verdict either way.

vectors.name: duty-short-of-the-period-it-states
vectors.note: A whole pack whose `held` figure is younger than the `required` period its own revision names. The document is not at fault and the reader has no opinion to hand back: `met` is absent from the format so that a deployment signs evidence rather than its own conclusion, and the arithmetic belongs to whoever holds the mapping.

vectors.name: unprotected-map-carries-a-parameter
vectors.note: The honest document with the unprotected map filled instead of left empty. That map is the one place in this container a signer fills at will: it sits outside the signature, so nothing written in it travels as a claim about the span, and enforcing that it is empty would buy strictness with no security content behind it.

vectors.name: stamps-run-backwards-accepted
vectors.note: The two orders a pack carries, disagreeing. The store chains a receipt under whatever stamp it was handed, so a deployment that corrected its clock produces this document: the links ascend, the stamps descend, and every record digest comes out. It is accepted and the disagreement is reported as a finding naming the step, because refusing it would reject lawful output on a ground no rule of this format states.

vectors.name: two-records-under-one-stamp
vectors.note: A store that served two records inside the same second chains them under one stamp, and the links still order them. Equal stamps are not a disagreement, so this row is accepted with no finding beside it: a reader that reported equality as an ordering fault would bury the steps where the two orders really do part.

vectors.name: provenance-live-run
vectors.note: Every record of this pack states that a running deployment produced its material while answering a real request, and the pack states live as well, which is the value its items reduce to. The receipts are this suite's fixtures like every row here and the one thing this row moves about them is what they declare about their own execution: a software measurement, the claim a deployment with no hardware protection makes. The pair of statements is the separation the field keeps and not a contradiction: a live origin says where the material came from, it does not make the run hardware evidence, and the receipt's own measurement is where that separate claim lives. The bytes pin the shape such a pack takes and the reduction the reader checks, and the provenance field itself is the writer's signed statement, which no reader recomputes.

vectors.name: provenance-captured-replay
vectors.note: Every record states that its material is a vendor-signed document recorded elsewhere and replayed into a locally issued receipt, and the pack states the captured value those items reduce to. The receipts keep the corpus' hardware measurement, because that is what the captured shape is: the vendor signature behind the document is real and the receipt around it is this deployment's, which is a valid piece of hardware evidence and is not a live run. The row is the second half of the pair the two sentences state: live software never becomes hardware evidence, and a captured original retains valid hardware evidence.

vectors.name: provenance-mixture-reduces-to-the-weakest
vectors.note: A pack whose first and third records state a live origin and whose middle record states a capture, sealed with the value its items reduce to: captured. This is the mixture cell the reduction exists for. The captured item is not washed down to live by the live items beside it, because the weakest value wins and the captured item is the weakest, and the pack cannot state live for the whole while the middle record carries that capture. The run is otherwise the honest three-record span every accepted row starts from, so what this row publishes is the reduction and nothing else.

vectors.name: shortened-run-closing-at-its-own-head
vectors.note: The middle record lifted out and the run re-chained to the head that shorter run hashes to, which is what a deployment that removed a receipt and re-signed the endpoints would hand over. Every check the container supports passes and the deletion is invisible from these bytes alone: publishing the head makes deletion detectable against a copy a reader held from before, and this reader is handed none. The run it reports is two items, and the window it states is the window it was signed to answer for.

vectors.name: no-designation-at-all
vectors.note: The honest document and a call that handed the reader neither a pinned key nor a resolver. The fault is in the call, so it is answered before a byte is read: a document question about bytes nobody has been given a key to check would send an operator to the pack rather than to their own configuration.

vectors.name: sealed-under-another-deployment-key
vectors.note: The honest manifest sealed by a key this reader was not given, under that key's own kid. The bytes are a whole pack and their signature holds against the header that names them; the refusal is that this caller does not designate that key, which is a different finding from tampering and the reason the two are separate codes.

vectors.name: header-naming-one-key-signed-by-another
vectors.note: A protected header carrying the designated kid and a signature the designated key did not make, which is the shape that separates a wrong key from an edited document. The kid check passes and the signature is what refuses, so the report is about tampering.
vectors.edited: the private half that made the signature, with the header naming the other key

vectors.name: receipt-byte-changed-after-sealing
vectors.note: One byte of the first item's receipt flipped after the document was signed, with the old signature left in place. The manifest still decodes and every width and relation in it holds, because the receipt bytes are opaque to the structure and inside the hash of the record they belong to, so what refuses is the signature and nothing else.
vectors.edited: the thirteenth byte of items[0].receipt, under the signature made for it

vectors.name: protected-content-type-of-a-receipt
vectors.note: The pack manifest inside an envelope whose `typ` is the receipt's. Both containers are `COSE_Sign1` over four elements signed by this same key and each verifies cleanly under it, so the mistake a content type exists to prevent is exactly this one, and it is refused at the header before any resolver is consulted.
vectors.edited: typ, from ashaveri/pack to ashaveri/receipt

vectors.name: protected-content-type-of-an-export
vectors.note: That same pair in the other direction, under the export type, which is the third container one deployment key signs. A reader that answered with the document it was hoping for would be reporting the wrong claim under a signature that held.
vectors.edited: typ, from ashaveri/pack to ashaveri/export

vectors.name: protected-header-carries-a-fourth-label
vectors.note: A protected header carrying a label this format does not declare, beside the three it does, and signed over as always. The header closes where a reader might be tempted to be open, because its bytes are hashed into the `Sig_structure`: a fourth label is an authenticated parameter and a reader that took the three it knows would hand on a document other than the one the deployment signed.
vectors.edited: a fourth protected label, 5, carrying a tstr

vectors.name: protected-kid-of-another-width
vectors.note: A `kid` of thirty-one bytes, a declared label holding the wrong shape. The width is what makes the field an id at all: it is sha256 of a public key, and a reader that took a shorter one would be resolving a key from bytes nothing hashes to.
vectors.edited: the protected kid, one byte short of the digest it is meant to be

vectors.name: protected-alg-naming-another-suite
vectors.note: An `alg` of -7 where this container signs with EdDSA. The header refusal and this one are separate codes on purpose: one says the map is not the map this format declares, the other says the map is right and names a suite nothing here produces.
vectors.edited: alg, from -8 to -7

vectors.name: manifest-version-no-format-has-used
vectors.note: A manifest declaring a pack version no format has used. The answer is about the reach of this reader rather than about the bytes being broken, and it arrives with no key in hand because a version is a fact of the document.
vectors.edited: v, from 2 to 3

vectors.name: manifest-member-unknown-to-this-version
vectors.note: A manifest carrying a member this version names nowhere. The map is closed, so the document is malformed rather than read with the unexpected member dropped: a member a reader ignores is a claim inside the signature that nobody looked at.
vectors.edited: a member named 'met' added to the manifest

vectors.name: item-stamped-outside-its-span
vectors.note: One item whose stamp is at the excluded end of the span the same signature states. Both bounds bind every item, which is the set the store's own range query serves for those two stamps, so this is two signed members contradicting each other and not a deployment that failed to hold what it answered for.
vectors.edited: items[2].iat, to the instant the span excludes

vectors.name: assembly-before-the-span-closed
vectors.note: A pack whose reads began before the window it answers for ended. A span still receiving has no completeness for a deployment to have signed, and both stamps are inside one signature, so the disagreement is the document's and is refused whoever signed it.
vectors.edited: at, to one second before the span closed

vectors.name: revision-after-the-reads
vectors.note: A duty mapping revision that postdates the instant the assembly began, which is not the revision the period was read from. Without this the artifact would date its own conclusion by the day somebody opened it.
vectors.edited: duty.rev, to one second after at

vectors.name: held-younger-than-the-oldest-item
vectors.note: A `held` figure below the age of the oldest receipt this pack carries. The duty runs against everything still retained and the oldest item need not be it, but a pack covering a receipt is a statement that the store held that receipt, so a smaller figure contradicts the document carrying it.
vectors.edited: duty.held, to two seconds where the oldest item is three

vectors.name: no-items-at-all
vectors.note: A pack with an empty items array. Its walk would be vacuous, its head would equal its anchor, and the artifact would read as evidence while proving only that somebody signed two digests. That a window held nothing is a statement about the window and belongs to the artifact that states windows.
vectors.edited: the items array, emptied

vectors.name: stamp-spelled-as-a-float
vectors.note: An item stamp written as the half-precision float 1.0 of the integer it stands for... rather than as an integer. A float is a different major type and the only reader that can ever tell them apart is one reading the bytes, because a decoder that hands both over as one number leaves a check placed afterwards nothing to distinguish. The refusal is the format's integer rule, and it arrives where the bytes are decoded.
vectors.edited: items[1].iat, written as the float of a whole number

vectors.name: two-items-answering-to-one-name
vectors.note: The same `id` carried by two items, chained honestly over the records as given so that every link is right. The name sits inside the hash, so both spellings hash perfectly and nothing about a chain reports the collision; a refusal that names an item would otherwise mean whichever of the two a reader met first.

vectors.name: provenance-stronger-than-the-weakest-item
vectors.note: A pack whose every record is a fixture, sealed with a statement that its material is a live run. The member is a reduction and not a parameter, so the document contradicts itself and a reader refuses it whoever signed it: a stronger value would claim more than the pack carries, and the stronger direction is the one the design's exit test names, a pack whose top-level provenance is stronger than its weakest item. The writer refuses to seal these bytes at all, which is why the row is assembled from the pieces and published as the document a port has to answer.
vectors.edited: prov, stated as live where the weakest item is a fixture

vectors.name: provenance-label-outside-the-three
vectors.note: A record carrying a provenance label this version defines no reading for. The vocabulary is closed, and the refusal is the member not being the one this version declares rather than a guess at which of the three the writer meant: a reader that read the value as whichever it resembled would be reporting a provenance no document stated.
vectors.edited: items[1].prov, set to a label outside the three

vectors.name: item-receipt-is-not-a-receipt
vectors.note: An item whose `receipt` is a sentence rather than a signed document. The originals are read before the walk, so what a caller hears is that this pack carries something other than the receipts it claims, and the refusal names which item and with what answer.

vectors.name: item-chained-under-a-stamp-it-does-not-attest
vectors.note: The middle item restamped to a value its own receipt does not carry, with its successor's link and the head recomputed over the moved stamp so that the run closes at the stamp it now states. The store chains under the stamp it was handed, so the item's `iat` and the receipt's are two statements and their equality is part of the walk: this is a receipt moved into a window it was never issued in, and nothing else in these bytes says so.
vectors.edited: items[1].iat, one second past the stamp its receipt attests, and the successor relinked over it

vectors.name: record-lifted-out-of-the-middle
vectors.note: The middle record taken out of a signed run and nothing else touched, so the successor still names the predecessor it had and the head is the one the whole run hashed to. What remains is whole by its own digest and the walk stops at the hole, which is the deletion publishing the head inside the signature exists to make visible.
vectors.edited: the items array, with the middle record removed

vectors.name: two-items-naming-one-predecessor
vectors.note: A second item claiming the anchor as its predecessor, the rest of the run untouched. The walk would take whichever it met first and report the other as unreached, so a fork is refused rather than resolved by the order the array happened to be in.
vectors.edited: a rival item chained from the same anchor as the first record

vectors.name: item-parked-beside-the-run
vectors.note: A receipt handed over beside a run it is not part of, naming a predecessor nobody here carries. The walk reaches the signed head and never had to visit it, so the count of what the walk reached against the array is the half of the rule with eyes for it, and a verifier that implements only the walk passes this pack.
vectors.edited: a fourth item chained from a digest no item in this run carries

vectors.name: custody-entry-answers-for-no-held-slot
vectors.note: custody[1] names `receipt-9` at `val`, and this pack seals no such record. The body digest it states is the digest a real slot of another record states, so the entry is a record of an observation nobody asked this pack to stand behind, which is the other direction from falling short and a different construction to fix. The refusal lands on the entry and quotes the slot it claims and the digest it states.
vectors.edited: custody[1].k.item, a record this pack does not seal

vectors.name: held-slot-no-custody-entry-answers-for
vectors.note: The same run and the same material, with the reference answering receipt-2 at `val` taken out. Every entry left answers a real slot, so nothing here is surplus: the pack seals a receipt that states material it took in and signs nothing about it, which is the pack's own defect and never a statement that the material is missing from the world. The refusal names the item, the slot and the digest it cannot answer for.
vectors.edited: the custody list, with the entry receipt-2 names at val removed

vectors.name: one-custody-entry-for-two-held-slots
vectors.note: The run whose two anchor slots digest one body, answered once: the list carries the entry for `col` and nothing for `val`, though both state the same digest. No entry here names a slot that is not held and none misstates a digest, so this is not the refusal for an entry answering to nothing; the pack seals a receipt stating a held slot and signs no reference for it, which is the pack falling short of a slot it did state. The sentence names the half it stopped on and the digest it cannot answer for, which is the very digest the answered half states, so a reader can see that the shortage is about the slot and not about the material.
vectors.edited: the custody list, answering one pair of held slots that state one digest with a single entry

vectors.name: custody-instant-outside-the-band
vectors.note: custody[0].s is the honest instant written in milliseconds, which is a whole number no earlier than the epoch and indistinguishable from a reading of seconds by its value alone. The band the receipt format draws for a Unix second is the only thing that can tell the two units apart, so the refusal lands on the reading before any member of the material is weighed and states both ends. `custody[0].w` is untouched, so this is the unit and nothing else.
vectors.edited: custody[0].s, the same instant a thousand times over

vectors.name: custody-window-outside-the-band
vectors.note: The same fault at the other member the rule reads: custody[0].w.to is a millisecond spelling beside an honest `s` and an honest window start. The window is the document's own signed statement, and a reader that weighed one end in seconds and the other in a thousandths of a second would be reporting a standing period it had not read.
vectors.edited: custody[0].w.to, the window ended in milliseconds

vectors.name: attached-entry-misstates-its-own-bytes
vectors.note: attached[1] holds the validity window and states the digest of the TCB info, which is the object at attached[0]. The reader recomputes rather than adjudicating between the two claims inside one entry, so the refusal lands on position 1 and quotes both digests: an arm that is wrong about the bytes it is holding is not evidence about anything else either.
vectors.edited: attached[1].sha256, the digest of attached[0] bytes rather than of the bytes beside it

vectors.name: attached-list-holds-one-object-twice
vectors.note: attached[1] repeats attached[0] in full, bytes, header and digests, and the TCB info those two entries hold is the body digest of three references. Deduplication is inside the pack, so one object is attached once however many references name it, and the second copy makes the length of the arm stop meaning the material the pack holds. The refusal names both positions and the digest.
vectors.edited: attached[1], a second entry for the object already at attached[0]

vectors.name: attached-entry-no-reference-names
vectors.note: A fourth object beside the three that resolve, holding material no reference of this pack states as its body digest. The three honest positions are untouched, so this is the pack attaching more than it speaks of rather than short of what it speaks of, which is why the refusal is a different code from the one that names a slot: it lands on attached[3] and the action is to drop that entry or sign the reference it belongs to.
vectors.edited: attached[3], an object the body digest of no reference names

vectors.name: attached-header-states-no-digest
vectors.note: attached[0] carries the issuer chain header and states no digest for it. The two halves of that pair are one statement, so a header arriving alone is the document contradicting itself about a member of its own arm, and no recomputation can settle which half the issuer meant; the refusal is the malformed-manifest code and it lands before anything is hashed.
vectors.edited: attached[0].chain_sha256, nulled beside a header that is still there

vectors.name: attached-header-no-reference-states
vectors.note: attached[2] carries a header and states its digest, and both are true of the bytes beside them, while the reference this object resolves to states `c: null`: the capture that read this document weighed it with the certificates inside it and no header arrived at all. An arm cannot add a chain to a reading that saw none, so the refusal names the position, the reference and what each of the two states.
vectors.edited: attached[2].chain, a header the reference it resolves to states no digest for

vectors.name: custody-arm-chain-mismatch
vectors.note: The served pack above with attached[0].chain swapped for another answer's header: the body still hashes to the digest three references state, the header still hashes to the digest the entry states for it, and what disagrees is that header against the digest those references state for the header that arrived beside the body. The reader recomputes both halves, weighs them against the reference each resolves to, and refuses the pair naming the position, the header the arm carried in full and the reference it weighed it against, whose own digest reaches the head of it before the bound the format puts on every quoted detail stops the sentence. An arm mistaken about which chain came with a document is not evidence about the document either, and nothing short of recomputing both halves and comparing the pair says so.
vectors.edited: attached[0].chain, the header of another answer attached beside this body

vectors.name: envelope-without-its-tag
vectors.note: The four elements of a `COSE_Sign1` with the tag around them missing, which is a shape a reader cannot recover by being tolerant: tag 18 is what says these bytes are an envelope at all.
vectors.edited: the CBOR tag 18 around the four envelope elements

vectors.name: envelope-whose-signature-is-not-64-bytes
vectors.note: The honest envelope with one byte taken off the end of its signature, which is a shape refusal rather than a cryptography failure: a reader that reached the verification step with a truncated signature would be reporting a wrong answer about the wrong bytes.
vectors.edited: the last byte of the signature

vectors.name: document-truncated-mid-envelope
vectors.note: The first twenty-four bytes of a whole pack, so nothing decodes and no header, key or manifest is ever reached.

crossReading.note: Four containers, one signing key, and each reader refusing the others' document at its protected header before a key is consulted. The pack half of that pair is in the rows named `protected-content-type-*`; these are the pack document given to the reader of an export, which is the confusion the content type exists to prevent.

cases.name: pack-read-as-export
cases.note: The honest pack, handed to the export reader under the key it names. The envelope decodes, the signature holds, and the typ is not the export's, so the answer is the header refusal rather than a manifest problem these bytes do not have.
